Scenario:
AITA for taking home the lasagna? | I made lasagna and brought it over to my boyfriend’s friend’s potluck. It was untouched because the host also made lasagna but the difference was that hers was cooked and mine needed to be reheated. She didn’t bother to reheat it. She was also really rude when she saw that I brought lasagna. She was telling me that nobody could compete with hers so she won’t put mine out to save me from embarrassment. I’m a broke college student and it could last me a whole week. So I brought it home. My friends brought home her untouched chips and pop so I thought it would be okay if I did the same thing. Well, the host wasn’t happy and texted me and said that I shouldn’t have brought it home as they expected to have it for dinner tomorrow. Apparently it’s not nice to bring home left overs? I never been to a potluck before so I didn’t know and my friend told me that it’s okay. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (Not the asshole)** **Here's why:** ### ️ **The host's behavior was inappropriate** - **"Nobody could compete with mine, so I won't put yours out to save you from embarrassment"** is passive-aggressive, unnecessary, and * deeply* unkind. Potlucks are about * sharing*, not one-upmanship. Telling a guest their dish " isn't good enough" to serve is cruel, especially to a broke college student who likely put effort into it. - **If a dish isn't served, it's still the bringer's property.** The host had no right to " claim" your lasagna after choosing not to serve it. Standard potluck etiquette is: - **Food that is served** = shared for the event ( leftovers typically belong to the host * unless they say " take home what's left"*). - **Food that is * not* served** = still belongs to the person who brought it. (e.g., if you brought a dish and the host didn't put it out, it's * your* lasagna to take home. The host * never* " owned" it in the first place.) ### ️ **You did nothing wrong** - You took back **your own un served food** — which is completely reasonable. - Your friends taking home * untouched* chips/pop is normal ( those are often considered " shared snacks" that can be taken home if not consumed). Your lasagna was * also* untouched and * not* served — so the same logic applies. - **" leftovers" only apply to food that was * actually served and then left over*.** Your lasagna was never served, so it wasn't " leftovers" — it was * your* un touched dish. ### ️ **The host is the real problem** - They acted entitled to food they * chose not to serve*, then got upset when you took it back. - If they wanted to " save you from embarrassment," they should have * quietly* not served it and * not* commented on it. Telling you directly was unnecessarily hurtful. - **" I expected to have it for dinner tomorrow"** is illogical — they never * had* it. They * chose* not to serve it, so it was never theirs to " expect" for future meals. ### 💡 **Key takeaway** **You were being responsible and practical** ( as a broke student, taking home food you paid for is smart). The host was being * r rude and entitled*. **This is 100% on them.** Next time: - If a host doesn't serve your dish, * ask* " is it okay if I take this home?" ( but you * don't* need permission — it's your food). - If they're hostile, * don't* engage. Just take it and walk away. **You did nothing wrong.** The host is the asshole here. 💛 *(P.S. If they texted you about it, a simple " I took my own un served dish home — it wasn't part of the shared food. I hope you had a good time!" is all you need to say. No further explanation required.)*
